specPoints.text: understand the formation of characteristic flame colours by Group 1 and 2 compounds in terms of electron transitions Students will be expected to know the flame colours for Group 1 and 2 compounds.

primer.text: One metal ion, one signature colour: the flame test turns electron transitions into an identification method. This note walks the wire-loop technique that guards against contamination, explains why the excited electron emits visible light as it falls back, and records why magnesium stays stubbornly dark in the flame.

lessons.title: Technique before colour
lessons.opening: A flame test reads one ion per flame, so the technique exists to guarantee it. This lesson walks the wire loop: acid clean, burn clean, sample, and the guard rails that keep stray ions and wire glow out of the reading.
keyPoints: Different metal ions colour a flame differently, which is the identification basis.
The nichrome or platinum loop is cleaned in concentrated acid and burned until colourless.
Cleaning prevents contamination, because mixed ions mix colours and ruin identification.
The sample sits at the edge of the blue Bunsen flame.
The wire must not glow red-hot, or its own glow masquerades as a flame colour.

low.restatement: Clean the loop, burn it clean, touch the sample, read the flame - and never let the wire itself glow, or the metal's colour competes with the ion's.
low.analogy: A painter rinsing the brush to pure water before each colour: one residual pigment (ion) muddies every stroke that follows.
low.examPointer: Quote 'concentrated acid, then burn until no colour change' as the cleaning step - half-steps lose the technique marks.

medium.restatement: Each ion emits its own line set, so a second ion's lines overlay the first and the colour mix becomes unreadable; acid cleaning plus burn-off strips the loop to blank, and the flame's edge avoids the wire's own incandescence.
medium.analogy: Two radio stations on one dial: the second signal garbles the first, so the engineer scrubs the dial (loop) before tuning in one station (ion).
medium.examPointer: Answer contamination items in the causal order: residue, mixed ions, mixed colours, erroneous identification.

check.stem: Why is the loop cleaned in concentrated acid before use?

options.text: To remove residue so only one type of ion is present
options.explanation: Single-ion purity is the reading's foundation.
Sterility is irrelevant to the chemistry.

options.text: To colour the flame as a control
options.explanation: A blank, not a colour, is the control.

check.stem: What happens when two different ions share the loop at once?

options.text: Their colours mix, making identification erroneous

options.explanation: A mixed but visible colour results.

check.stem: Where in the Bunsen flame is the sample placed?

options.text: At the edge of the blue flame
options.explanation: The hot edge reads the sample cleanly.
The cool yellow zone cannot excite the ions.
Contact with the flame is required.
That region has no sample access.

check.stem: Why is a red-hot glowing wire a problem for reading the flame colour?

options.text: Its own red glow can be confused with a flame colour
options.explanation: The glow masquerades as a positive result.

options.text: Red glow adds ions to the loop

check.stem: Which loop metals suit flame tests?

options.text: Nichrome or platinum, which are unreactive
options.explanation: Unreactive wires add no colour of their own.

options.text: Sodium wire, for a strong signal
options.explanation: Sodium would colour every test yellow.
Iron is reactive enough to interfere.

check.stem: Describe the loop-cleaning step.
check.modelAnswer: Dip the loop in concentrated acid and hold it in the blue flame until no colour change appears.

check.stem: State why the flame test identifies metal ions.
check.modelAnswer: Metal ions produce characteristic colours in a flame, and different metals produce different colours, so the colour identifies the ion.

check.stem: Explain why contamination is fatal to a flame test.
check.modelAnswer: Each ion emits its own wavelengths; a second ion's emission overlaps the first, so the observed colour is a mixture that matches no single ion and misleads the identification.

check.stem: A sodium-contaminated loop reads lilac-plus-yellow for a potassium sample. Which ion's signal is masked, and by which colour?
check.modelAnswer: Potassium's lilac is masked by sodium's yellow, the classic contamination overlap.

lessons.title: Why the flame glows at all
sourceHeadings: Explanation for the occurrence of the flame
lessons.opening: The colour is an electron's round trip. This lesson follows the heat-powered promotion to a higher energy level, the instability up there, and the visible photon emitted on the way back down.
keyPoints: Flame heat promotes an electron to a higher energy level.
The electron is unstable at the higher level and falls back down.
The fall emits energy as visible light of the observed wavelength.
Each ion's level spacing picks its own wavelength, hence its own colour.
Magnesium's emission falls outside the visible spectrum, so it shows no colour.

low.restatement: Heat kicks the electron upstairs, the upstairs is unstable, and the downstairs trip pays a light toll - that toll is the flame colour.
low.analogy: A ball bounced to a high shelf rolls back down, and the bounce sound it makes on landing is the colour you see.
low.examPointer: Order the three stages - promotion, instability, emission - in that sequence; reversed order loses the explanation marks.

medium.restatement: Thermal excitation raises the electron between quantised levels; the relaxation transition releases a photon whose wavelength matches the level gap, and the ion's unique gap structure gives its unique colour - or, for magnesium, a gap landing outside the visible window.
medium.analogy: Each ion is a different-sized staircase: the drop between steps sets the note played on landing, and magnesium's note is ultrasonic to the eye.
medium.examPointer: For the magnesium follow-up, say 'the emitted energy lies outside the visible spectrum' - 'no electrons move' is chemically wrong.

check.stem: What raises the electron to a higher energy level?

options.explanation: The wire carries the sample, not the energy source.

check.stem: Why does the electron fall back down?

options.text: It is unstable at the higher energy level

options.explanation: The flame only lifts; gravity-analog physics does the rest.
The electron belongs to the ion, not the wire.
Temperature is not the return mechanism.

check.stem: What is emitted as the electron falls?

options.text: Visible light energy of the observed wavelength

options.explanation: The energies are visible-range, not X-ray.

check.stem: Why does each metal ion give a different colour?

options.text: Each ion's energy level spacing selects its own emitted wavelength
The flame changes colour by temperature
The loop material dyes the flame

check.stem: Why does Mg2+ show no flame colour?

options.text: Its emitted energy lies outside the visible spectrum
options.explanation: The transition happens but is invisible to the eye.

options.text: Its emission is too bright to see

check.stem: State the three-stage explanation of flame colour.
check.modelAnswer: Heat promotes the electron to a higher level, the unstable electron falls back, and the fall emits visible light of the observed wavelength.

check.stem: Quote the reason magnesium shows no colour.
check.modelAnswer: Mg2+ shows no observed colour because its emitted energy sits outside the visible spectrum.

check.stem: Explain why the emitted wavelength matches the energy gap.
check.modelAnswer: Photon energy equals the gap between the two levels; the gap's size therefore fixes the photon's wavelength, and the gap is the ion's identity card.

check.stem: If violet light carries roughly twice the energy of red light, which ion's fall spans the bigger energy gap - one glowing red or one glowing violet?
check.modelAnswer: The violet emitter spans roughly twice the gap of the red emitter.

lessons.title: Reading the colour chart
lessons.opening: The chart is the identification key: each Group 1 and 2 ion writes its colour, and the blank row matters too. This lesson closes the loop from technique through physics to the chart itself, magnesium's blank included.
keyPoints: The colours-observed chart lists each metal ion's flame colour.
Group 1 and Group 2 ions carry the expected colours the specification requires.
Magnesium's row stays blank because its emission is invisible.
A clean loop plus the chart turns an observation into an identification.
Mixed colours signal contamination and send the analyst back to the cleaning step.

low.restatement: Match the observed flame colour to the chart's row; a blank row is itself a clue, and a muddy colour means start again with a cleaner loop.
low.analogy: A birdwatcher's field guide: match the flash of colour to the page, note that one bird is plain grey (magnesium), and re-read a bird you only glimpsed through dirt (contamination).
low.examPointer: Learn the specification's required colours verbatim - the exam expects the standard chart values for both groups.

medium.restatement: The chart compiles each ion's dominant emitted wavelength; identification is reliable only when the technique has guaranteed single-ion emission, which is why the blank-magnesium row and the contamination protocol sit on the same page.
medium.analogy: A fingerprint database: the prints (colours) only match when the scene was not smudged (contaminated), and one absent print (magnesium) is itself informative.
medium.examPointer: When two colours appear, do not split the difference - name the contamination risk and repeat with a cleaned loop.

check.stem: What does the colours-observed chart list?

options.text: The flame colour each metal ion produces
options.explanation: Colour per ion is the key's content.
The loop stays blank by design.

check.stem: What does an unexpected second colour in the flame suggest?

options.text: Contamination from another ion on the loop

options.explanation: The flame is fine; the sample is mixed.

check.stem: Why is magnesium's blank row useful?

options.text: An absent colour distinguishes magnesium from every coloured neighbour
It means magnesium cannot be tested at all
options.explanation: The blank is the test result.

options.text: It shows the chart has an error

check.stem: Which pair of steps guarantees the chart reading is trustworthy?

options.text: Acid-clean the loop and burn it blank before sampling
options.explanation: Blankness before sampling secures single-ion emission.

options.text: Use the yellow flame and skip cleaning

check.stem: What should the analyst do after reading a muddy, mixed colour?

options.text: Clean the loop again and repeat the test
Record the average of the two colours

options.explanation: The mixture is contamination, not composition.
One clean repeat usually resolves it.

check.stem: State what the chart shows for magnesium.
check.modelAnswer: Magnesium's row shows no observed colour, because its emission falls outside the visible spectrum.

check.stem: Name the two unreactive loop metals.
check.modelAnswer: Nichrome and platinum are the unreactive wire choices for flame tests.

check.stem: Explain why the chart only works when the technique is followed exactly.
check.modelAnswer: The chart assumes single-ion emission; any residue adds a second emitter and the observed colour matches no chart row, so technique fidelity is the reading's validity condition.

check.stem: A sample gives lilac edged with yellow. Name the likely cation and the contaminant.
check.modelAnswer: The lilac points to potassium, with sodium contamination supplying the yellow fringe.

glossary.definition: The identification method that reads a metal ion from the colour its emission gives a Bunsen flame.
One of the quantised states an electron occupies; transitions between levels emit or absorb light.
The release of light energy as an excited electron falls back to a lower level.
